#### Mock exam: Advanced Types and Async Mock Exam

*22 questions · 20 minutes · pass mark 70%.* Ten questions drawn from the level's bank, from conditional and mapped types to decorators, the event loop and testing.

**Question 1** · One answer · `ts-advanced-01`

```ts
interface Room {
  name: string;
  seats: number;
}
function field<T, K extends keyof T>(item: T, key: K): T[K] {
  return item[key];
}
const room: Room = { name: "Hall", seats: 120 };
const seats = field(room, "seats");
```

Which type does TypeScript infer for `seats`?

- **✔ A. `number`**
- B. `string | number`
- C. `Room[keyof Room]`
- D. `unknown`, because `T` could be anything inside `field`

> **Why:** `T` is inferred as `Room` from the first argument, and `K` as the literal type `"seats"`
> from the second, so the return type `T[K]` is `Room["seats"]`, which is `number`.
> `string | number` would be the result of `Room[keyof Room]`, which is what you get if the
> key parameter is typed `keyof T` instead of its own type parameter `K`: then the specific
> key is forgotten. Inside the function `T` is unknown, but at the call it is known.

**Question 2** · One answer · `ts-advanced-02`

```ts
interface Sink<in T> {
  write: (value: T) => void;
}
declare const textSink: Sink<string>;
declare const mixedSink: Sink<string | number>;
```

Which assignment compiles?

- **✔ A. `const a: Sink<string> = mixedSink;`**
- B. `const b: Sink<string | number> = textSink;`
- C. Both, because variance annotations are only documentation
- D. Neither, because `in` makes `Sink` invariant

> **Why:** A sink only takes values in, so it is **contravariant**: something that can write any
> `string | number` can certainly write a `string`, so a `Sink<string | number>` may be used
> as a `Sink<string>`. The reverse fails with error TS2322, "Type 'Sink<string>' is not
> assignable to type 'Sink<string | number>'", because a text-only sink cannot accept a number.
> `in` states contravariance and the compiler checks it; `in out` would mean invariant.

**Question 3** · Select all that apply · `ts-advanced-03`

```ts
function tags<const T extends readonly string[]>(list: T): T {
  return list;
}
const inline = tags(["jazz", "soul"]);
const stored = ["jazz", "soul"];
const fromVariable = tags(stored);
```

Which statements are true? Choose two.

- **✔ A. `inline` has the type `readonly ["jazz", "soul"]`**
- **✔ B. `fromVariable` has the type `string[]`**
- C. `fromVariable` has the type `readonly ["jazz", "soul"]`, because `const` applies to every argument
- D. `inline` has the type `string[]`, because `const` on a type parameter only forbids reassignment

> **Why:** A `const` type parameter makes inference treat literals **written in the call** as if they
> had `as const`, so `inline` is the readonly tuple `readonly ["jazz", "soul"]`. It has no
> effect on a value that already has a type: `stored` was inferred as `string[]` when it was
> declared, so `fromVariable` is `string[]`. The `readonly string[]` constraint matters too:
> it lets the readonly tuple satisfy the constraint.

**Question 4** · One answer · `ts-advanced-04`

```ts
type Wrap<T> = T extends unknown ? { value: T } : never;
type W = Wrap<"a" | 1>;
```

What is `W`?

- **✔ A. `{ value: "a" } | { value: 1 }`**
- B. `{ value: "a" | 1 }`
- C. `never`, because a union does not extend `unknown`
- D. `{ value: unknown }`

> **Why:** The checked type is a bare type parameter, so the conditional type is **distributive**: it
> is applied to `"a"` and to `1` separately and the results are joined into a union. To check
> the union as a whole and get `{ value: "a" | 1 }`, wrap both sides in brackets:
> `[T] extends [unknown] ? { value: T } : never`. Every type extends `unknown`, so `never` is
> never chosen here.

**Question 5** · One answer · `ts-advanced-05`

```ts
type ElementType<T> = T extends readonly (infer E)[] ? E : never;
type A = ElementType<number[]>;
type B = ElementType<string>;
```

What are `A` and `B`?

- **✔ A. `A` is `number`, `B` is `never`**
- B. `A` is `number`, `B` is `string`, because a string is a sequence of characters
- C. `A` is `number[]`, `B` is `never`
- D. `A` is `unknown`, because `infer` cannot see inside arrays

> **Why:** `infer E` captures whatever stands in the element position when `T` matches the pattern
> `readonly E[]`. `number[]` matches, so `A` is `number`. `string` is not an array type (being
> iterable is not enough), so the false branch gives `never`, and assigning `"x"` to a `B` is
> error TS2322, "Type '"x"' is not assignable to type 'never'."

**Question 6** · One answer · `ts-advanced-06`

```ts
type IsString<T> = T extends string ? true : false;
type R = IsString<never>;
```

What is `R`?

- **✔ A. `never`**
- B. `true`, because `never` is assignable to every type
- C. `false`, because `never` is not a string
- D. `boolean`

> **Why:** `IsString` is distributive, and `never` is the empty union: distributing over no members
> gives no results, which is `never`. Even `const r: R = true` is rejected with "Type 'true' is
> not assignable to type 'never'." `true` would be right for the non-distributive form
> `[T] extends [string] ? true : false`, since `never` is assignable to `string`. That
> bracketed form is how an `IsNever` check must be written.

**Question 7** · One answer · `ts-advanced-07`

```ts
type Methods<T> = { [K in keyof T as T[K] extends (...args: never[]) => unknown ? K : never]: T[K] };
interface Player {
  name: string;
  volume: number;
  play(): void;
  stop(): void;
}
type M = keyof Methods<Player>;
```

What is `M`?

- **✔ A. `"play" | "stop"`**
- B. `"name" | "volume" | "play" | "stop"`, because `as` only renames keys
- C. `"name" | "volume"`
- D. `never`, because a mapped type cannot inspect property types

> **Why:** The `as` clause computes each new key. For a property whose type is a function the
> conditional type gives back the key `K`; for the others it gives `never`, and a key remapped
> to `never` is dropped. So only the methods remain. The pattern
> `(...args: never[]) => unknown` matches every function, whatever its parameters.

**Question 8** · Select all that apply · `ts-advanced-08`

```ts
type Axis = "x" | "y";
type Edge = "start" | "end";
type Inset = `${Axis}-${Edge}`;
```

Which assignments compile? Choose two.

- **✔ A. `const a: Inset = "x-start";`**
- **✔ B. `const b: Inset = "y-end";`**
- C. `const c: Inset = "x-middle";`
- D. `const d: Inset = "xy-start";`

> **Why:** A template literal type with unions in its placeholders is every combination: here the four
> strings `"x-start"`, `"x-end"`, `"y-start"` and `"y-end"`. `"x-middle"` and `"xy-start"`
> are rejected, and TypeScript 7 lists the members in its stable order:
> `'"x-end" | "x-start" | "y-end" | "y-start"'`, adding "Did you mean '"x-start"'?" for the
> near miss.

**Question 9** · Select all that apply · `ts-advanced-09`

```ts
declare const brand: unique symbol;
type Meters = number & { readonly [brand]: "Meters" };
function meters(value: number): Meters {
  return value as Meters;
}
function climb(height: Meters): string {
  return `${height} m`;
}
const peak = meters(8848);
climb(peak);              // A
climb(8848);              // B
const plain: number = peak; // C
climb(peak + 1);          // D
```

Which lines does the compiler reject? Choose two.

- **✔ A. B**
- **✔ B. D**
- C. A
- D. C

> **Why:** A plain `number` lacks the brand property, so `climb(8848)` is rejected with "Argument of
> type 'number' is not assignable to parameter of type 'Meters'." Arithmetic returns a plain
> `number`, so `peak + 1` has lost the brand too (D). A branded value is still a `number`, so
> it can be assigned to one (C). Code that computes a new branded value must pass it through
> the validating function again.

**Question 10** · One answer · `ts-advanced-10`

```ts
const sizes = { small: 8, large: 16 } satisfies Record<string, number>;
type SizeName = keyof typeof sizes;

const annotated: Record<string, number> = { small: 8, large: 16 };
type AnnotatedName = keyof typeof annotated;
```

What are `SizeName` and `AnnotatedName`?

- **✔ A. `SizeName` is `"small" | "large"`; `AnnotatedName` is `string`**
- B. Both are `string`, because `satisfies` and an annotation give the same type
- C. Both are `"small" | "large"`
- D. `SizeName` is `string`; `AnnotatedName` is `"small" | "large"`

> **Why:** `satisfies` checks the object against `Record<string, number>` but leaves its type as
> inferred, `{ small: number; large: number }`, so its keys are `"small" | "large"`. An
> annotation replaces the inferred type with `Record<string, number>`, whose keys are any
> `string`; `annotated.medium` then compiles and is `undefined` at run time.

**Question 11** · One answer · `ts-advanced-11`

```ts
function toList(value: string): string[];
function toList(value: string[]): string[];
function toList(value: string | string[]): string[] {
  return typeof value === "string" ? [value] : value;
}
function normalize(input: string | string[]): string[] {
  return toList(input);
}
```

What happens when this is compiled?

- **✔ A. Error TS2769, "No overload matches this call", on `toList(input)`**
- B. It compiles, because the implementation signature accepts `string | string[]`
- C. It compiles, and TypeScript picks the first overload because `string` comes first
- D. An error on the implementation, because it is not compatible with the overloads

> **Why:** Callers see only the overload signatures, never the implementation's, and each call must
> match one overload on its own. A `string | string[]` argument fits neither `string` nor
> `string[]`. Since both overloads return `string[]`, the overloads add nothing: one signature
> with a union parameter is simpler and accepts every call. Otherwise, add a third overload
> taking the union.

**Question 12** · One answer · `ts-advanced-12`

```ts
const timer = {
  ticks: 0,
  tick(this: { ticks: number }): number {
    this.ticks++;
    return this.ticks;
  },
};
const tick = timer.tick;
console.log(tick());
```

What happens?

- **✔ A. A compile error: the `this` context of type `void` is not assignable to the method's `this`**
- B. It prints `1`
- C. It prints `NaN`, because `this` is the global object
- D. It compiles and then throws a `TypeError` at run time

> **Why:** The `this` parameter says the method must be called on an object with `ticks`. `tick()`
> calls it with no object, so the compiler reports error TS2684. Without the `this` parameter
> it would compile, and in an ES module `this` would be `undefined`, so `this.ticks++` would
> throw a `TypeError` at run time. Call `timer.tick()` or use `timer.tick.bind(timer)`.

**Question 13** · One answer · `ts-advanced-13`

```ts
interface Config {
  port: number;
}
interface Config {
  host: string;
}
const config: Config = { port: 8080 };
```

What does the compiler say?

- **✔ A. Property `host` is missing: the two declarations merged into one interface with both properties**
- B. Duplicate identifier `Config`
- C. Nothing: the second declaration replaces the first, so `{ port: 8080 }` is an excess property error at most
- D. Nothing: merged properties are optional

> **Why:** Interfaces with the same name in the same scope **merge**: `Config` has both `port` and
> `host`, so the object is rejected with error TS2741, "Property 'host' is missing in type
> '{ port: number; }' but required in type 'Config'." Type aliases do not merge: two
> `type Config` declarations are error TS2300, "Duplicate identifier 'Config'." Merging is
> what lets module augmentation add properties to a library's interfaces.

**Question 14** · One answer · `ts-advanced-14`

```ts
function announce(_method: unknown, context: ClassMethodDecoratorContext): void {
  console.log(`decorating ${String(context.name)}`);
}
console.log("before class");
class Box {
  @announce
  open(): void {
    console.log("open");
  }
}
console.log("after class");
new Box().open();
new Box().open();
```

Compiled with `tsc` and run with Node.js, what does it print?

- **✔ A. `before class`, `decorating open`, `after class`, `open`, `open`**
- B. `before class`, `after class`, `decorating open`, `open`, `decorating open`, `open`
- C. `decorating open`, `before class`, `after class`, `open`, `open`
- D. `before class`, `after class`, `open`, `open`, because a decorator that returns nothing is skipped

> **Why:** A decorator runs **once, when the class is defined**, which happens when execution reaches
> the class declaration, between the two `console.log` calls around it. Creating instances
> does not run it again. Returning nothing (`void`) keeps the original method, so `open` runs
> normally. Per-instance work belongs in `context.addInitializer` or in a replacement function.

**Question 15** · Select all that apply · `ts-advanced-15`

Which statements about standard (ECMAScript) decorators in TypeScript 7 and Node.js 26 are
true? Choose two.

- **✔ A. They need no compiler option; `experimentalDecorators` selects the older, different design**
- **✔ B. With `target: es2025`, `tsc` rewrites decorated classes into plain JavaScript with helper functions, which Node.js runs**
- C. Node.js 26 runs them directly from a `.ts` file by stripping them like types
- D. They can decorate parameters and support `emitDecoratorMetadata`

> **Why:** Standard decorators have been supported without a flag since TypeScript 5.0. JavaScript
> engines do not run decorators yet, so Node.js stops at the `@` with a syntax error when it
> strips types from a `.ts` file; compiling with `tsc` first emits helpers such as
> `__esDecorate`. Parameter decorators and `emitDecoratorMetadata` belong to the old
> `experimentalDecorators` design. For `context.metadata` on Node.js 26, `Symbol.metadata`
> must also be polyfilled before the class is defined.

**Question 16** · One answer · `ts-advanced-16`

```ts
console.log("1");
setImmediate(() => console.log("2"));
queueMicrotask(() => console.log("3"));
Promise.resolve().then(() => console.log("4"));
(async () => {
  console.log("5");
  await null;
  console.log("6");
})();
console.log("7");
```

In what order are the numbers printed?

- **✔ A. 1 5 7 3 4 6 2**
- B. 1 7 3 4 5 6 2
- C. 1 5 7 2 3 4 6
- D. 1 5 6 7 3 4 2

> **Why:** Synchronous code runs first: `1`, then the async function's body up to its first `await`
> (`5`), then `7`. The microtask queue is then drained in order: `3` and `4` were queued
> first, and the rest of the async function (`6`) was queued when it reached `await null`.
> `setImmediate` is a macrotask, so `2` comes last. An async function does not start later;
> it runs synchronously until its first `await`.

**Question 17** · One answer · `ts-advanced-17`

```ts
const first = new AbortController();
const second = new AbortController();
const either = AbortSignal.any([first.signal, second.signal]);
second.abort("second stopped");
first.abort("first stopped");
console.log(either.aborted, either.reason);
```

What does it print?

- **✔ A. `true second stopped`**
- B. `true first stopped`, because the first signal in the list wins
- C. `false undefined`, because the combined signal aborts only when all inputs abort
- D. `true [ 'second stopped', 'first stopped' ]`

> **Why:** `AbortSignal.any` returns a signal that aborts as soon as **any** input aborts, and its
> reason is the reason of the input that aborted first, whatever its position in the list.
> Aborting `first` later changes nothing: a signal aborts once. This is how a user's cancel
> button and a time limit (`AbortSignal.timeout`) are combined into one signal.

**Question 18** · One answer · `ts-advanced-18`

```ts
async function* count(): AsyncGenerator<number> {
  try {
    yield 1;
    yield 2;
    yield 3;
  } finally {
    console.log("cleanup");
  }
}
for await (const n of count()) {
  console.log(n);
  if (n === 2) break;
}
console.log("done");
```

What does it print?

- **✔ A. `1`, `2`, `cleanup`, `done`**
- B. `1`, `2`, `done`, because `break` leaves the generator suspended
- C. `1`, `2`, `3`, `cleanup`, `done`
- D. `1`, `2`, `done`, `cleanup`

> **Why:** Leaving a `for await` loop early calls the iterator's `return` method and waits for it. The
> generator resumes as if a `return` happened at its paused `yield`, so its `finally` block runs
> before the loop statement completes, and `3` is never produced. This is why an async
> generator can safely hold a resource (a file, a connection) and release it in `finally`.

**Question 19** · One answer · `ts-advanced-19`

```ts
type FetchError =
  | { kind: "offline" }
  | { kind: "not-found"; url: string }
  | { kind: "timeout"; seconds: number };

function message(error: FetchError): string {
  switch (error.kind) {
    case "offline":
      return "no connection";
    case "not-found":
      return `missing: ${error.url}`;
    default: {
      const unhandled: never = error;
      return unhandled;
    }
  }
}
```

What does the compiler report?

- **✔ A. An error on `const unhandled: never = error`: the `timeout` kind is not assignable to `never`**
- B. Nothing, because the `default` branch handles every remaining kind
- C. An error on the function: not all code paths return a value
- D. Nothing at compile time; the program throws when a timeout occurs

> **Why:** After the two `case`s, `error` has been narrowed to the members not yet handled. Here that is
> `{ kind: "timeout"; seconds: number }`, which cannot be assigned to `never`, so the compiler
> reports error TS2322 and names the forgotten kind. When every kind has a `case`, `error` is
> `never` in the `default` branch and the line compiles. A `default` that returns a fallback
> message would hide the missing case instead.

**Question 20** · One answer · `ts-advanced-20`

```ts
const outcomes = await Promise.allSettled([Promise.resolve(1), Promise.reject(new Error("b")), Promise.resolve(3)]);
console.log(outcomes.map((o) => o.status).join(" "));
try {
  await Promise.any([Promise.reject(new Error("a")), Promise.reject(new Error("b"))]);
} catch (error) {
  console.log(error instanceof AggregateError, (error as AggregateError).errors.length);
}
```

What does it print?

- **✔ A. `fulfilled rejected fulfilled`, then `true 2`**
- B. Only an unhandled rejection, because `allSettled` rejects with the first error
- C. `fulfilled rejected fulfilled`, then `false 2`, because `Promise.any` rejects with the last error
- D. `fulfilled fulfilled`, then `true 1`

> **Why:** `Promise.allSettled` never rejects: it reports every outcome in order, with a `status` of
> `"fulfilled"` or `"rejected"`. `Promise.any` resolves with the first success; when every
> promise rejects it rejects with an `AggregateError` whose `errors` hold all the reasons, in
> the order of the input. Node.js 26 gives it the message "All promises were rejected".

**Question 21** · One answer · `ts-advanced-21`

```ts
function double(value: number): number {
  return value * 2;
}
// @ts-expect-error double must reject a string
double("4");
// @ts-expect-error double must reject a number
double(4);
```

What does `tsc` report?

- **✔ A. Error TS2578, "Unused '@ts-expect-error' directive", for the second directive only**
- B. Nothing; `@ts-expect-error` only silences errors
- C. Error TS2345 for `double("4")`, because the directive only covers the next statement if it is a declaration
- D. Errors for both directives, because the reasons after them are not valid syntax

> **Why:** `@ts-expect-error` suppresses an error on the next line and **requires** that there be one.
> `double("4")` has an error, so the first directive is satisfied. `double(4)` is valid, so
> the second directive is unused, and `tsc` reports that. This is what makes it a type-level
> test: if a type becomes too loose, the directive above a misuse turns into an error. The
> text after the directive is a free comment.

**Question 22** · One answer · `ts-advanced-22`

```ts
import { mock } from "node:test";
const save = mock.fn((text: string) => text.length);
save("a");
save("bc");
console.log(save.mock.callCount(), save.mock.calls[1].arguments, save.mock.calls[1].result);
```

What does it print?

- **✔ A. `2 [ 'bc' ] 2`**
- B. `2 [ 'bc' ] undefined`, because a mock does not call its implementation
- C. `1 [ 'a' ] 1`, because `calls` is numbered from 1
- D. Nothing: `mock.fn` can only be used inside a `test` callback

> **Why:** `mock.fn(impl)` returns a function that calls `impl` and records each call: `callCount()`
> is 2, and `calls` is an ordinary array numbered from 0, so `calls[1]` is the second call,
> with its `arguments` and the `result` it returned. `mock` works outside a test too; inside
> one, `t.mock` is preferred because it restores everything when the test ends.

#### Lab: Playhouse Cue Bus

*TypeScript · about 55 minutes · 5 s per test.* Build a typed event bus for a theatre's show control, with payload and handler types derived from one event map, listeners that survive each other's failures, and a cancellable wait for the next cue.

**Scenario**

The Lantern Street Playhouse is a 180-seat theatre run by a small crew. During a performance the
stage manager sits at a desk in the wings and "calls the show": a standby warns the operators
that a cue is coming, and a go fires it. Three desks follow the calls. The lighting desk fades
the lamps, the sound desk plays effects, and the fly desk raises and lowers scenery on ropes.

```text
standby  { cue: 12 }
cueGo    { cue: 12, desk: "lights" }
cueGo    { cue: 12, desk: "sound" }
showStop { reason: "fire alarm" }
```

The playhouse is replacing its old show-control script. That script passed events around as
plain strings and objects, so a typo such as `"cuego"`, or a cue number sent as text, was only
found mid-performance. One desk's crash stopped the others from hearing the call. Its "wait for
the next cue" feature could not be cancelled, so after an emergency stop the stage stayed
blocked, waiting for a go that would never come.

You are writing the core of the new system: a typed event bus. The events of a show are
described once as a TypeScript type. From it, the compiler works out which events exist, which
payload each one carries, and what the desks' handler objects look like, so mistakes are caught
before the curtain goes up. At run time the bus calls listeners in a predictable order, keeps
going when one desk fails, and lets a desk wait for the next cue with a wait the stage manager
can cancel at once.

**Instructions**

Write `solution.ts`. The starter exports every name the tests import. Keep the names, the type
parameters and the method signatures of `CueBus`. You may add private fields, private methods
and helper types. The tests describe a show with this type:

```ts
type ShowEvents = {
  houseOpen: undefined;
  standby: { cue: number };
  cueGo: { cue: number; desk: "lights" | "sound" | "fly" };
  showStop: { reason: string };
};
```

Each key is an event name and its type is the event's payload. `undefined` means the event has
no payload.

**Types.** Hidden tests check them with `@ts-expect-error` and an exact type comparison, so a
type that is too loose fails even when the code runs.

1. `PayloadArgs<P>` is the tuple of arguments that follow the event name: `[]` when `P` is
   `undefined`, otherwise `[payload: P]`. An event whose payload type is `string | undefined`
   still takes exactly one argument, so `PayloadArgs<string | undefined>` is
   `[payload: string | undefined]` (lesson 2: watch out for distribution). `Listener<P>`, given,
   is built from it.
2. `Handlers<Events>` has one **optional** property per event, named `on` followed by the event
   name with its first letter in upper case, whose type is that event's `Listener`. For
   `ShowEvents` the keys are exactly `onHouseOpen`, `onStandby`, `onCueGo` and `onShowStop`, so
   `{ onCurtainUp: ... }` or `{ oncueGo: ... }` is rejected and `{}` is accepted.

**The bus.** `class CueBus<Events extends EventMap>` keeps its listeners per event name.

3. `on(name, listener)` adds a listener and returns a function that removes that registration.
   Adding the same function twice makes two registrations, each called on every emit and each
   removed by its own function. Calling a remove function a second time does nothing.
4. `emit(name, ...args)` calls the listeners of `name` that were registered **when the emit
   started**, in the order they were added, passing the payload (or nothing). A listener added or
   removed by another listener during an emit takes effect from the next emit. It returns the
   number of listeners it called (`0` if none).
   If any listeners throw, `emit` still calls all the others, then throws one `AggregateError`
   whose `errors` are the thrown values in order, with the message
   `` `${count} listener(s) failed on ${name}` ``.
5. `listenerCount(name)` returns how many registrations `name` has now.
6. `connect(handlers)` adds each handler that is a function as a listener of its event (the key
   without `on`, with the first letter in lower case: `onCueGo` listens to `cueGo`) and skips
   handlers that are `undefined`. It returns a function that removes exactly the listeners this
   call added; calling it again does nothing.
7. `next(name, options)` returns a promise for the payload of the next emit of `name` (or
   `undefined` for an event without a payload):
   - while it waits it is an ordinary registration: `listenerCount` counts it and `emit`
     includes it in the number it returns;
   - when the event arrives it removes its listener before resolving, so a later emit does not
     see it, and if it has a signal it removes its `abort` listener from the signal;
   - with `options.signal` already aborted, it rejects with `signal.reason` without adding a
     listener;
   - when the signal is aborted while it waits, it removes its listener at once and rejects with
     `signal.reason`. Listen with `signal.addEventListener("abort", ...)`.

Example, the start of opening night:

```ts
const bus = new CueBus<ShowEvents>();
const offLights = bus.on("cueGo", (payload) => console.log("lights", payload.cue));
bus.on("cueGo", (payload) => console.log("sound", payload.cue));
bus.emit("houseOpen");                         // 0: nobody listens yet
bus.emit("cueGo", { cue: 1, desk: "lights" }); // prints "lights 1", "sound 1"; returns 2
offLights();
bus.listenerCount("cueGo");                    // 1

const stop = new AbortController();
const nextStandby = bus.next("standby", { signal: stop.signal });
bus.emit("standby", { cue: 2 });               // returns 1: the waiting next
await nextStandby;                             // { cue: 2 }

bus.emit("cueGo");                             // compile error: cueGo needs its payload
bus.connect({ onCurtainUp: () => {} });        // compile error: no curtainUp event
```

**Tips.** Store each registration as its own small object, so removing one finds exactly it,
and copy the list before an emit loops over it. `Promise.withResolvers` keeps `next` short.
Write `PayloadArgs` with the non-distributive form from lesson 2, and build `Handlers` with key
remapping and `Capitalize` from lesson 3.

**Boilerplate given to the learner** (`starter.ts`)

```typescript
/** Event name to payload type. `undefined` means the event carries no payload. */
export type EventMap = Record<string, unknown>;

/**
 * Step 1: the arguments `emit` takes after the event name.
 * `[]` when the payload type is `undefined`, otherwise exactly one argument, `[payload: P]`.
 * An event whose payload type is `string | undefined` still takes one argument.
 */
export type PayloadArgs<P> = unknown[];

/** A listener receives the payload, or nothing for an event without one. */
export type Listener<P> = (...args: PayloadArgs<P>) => void;

/**
 * Step 2: one optional handler per event, named "on" followed by the event name with its first
 * letter in upper case (`cueGo` becomes `onCueGo`), typed as that event's Listener.
 */
export type Handlers<Events extends EventMap> = Record<string, unknown>;

export interface NextOptions {
  signal?: AbortSignal;
}

export class CueBus<Events extends EventMap> {
  on<K extends keyof Events & string>(name: K, listener: Listener<Events[K]>): () => void {
    throw new Error("Not implemented");
  }

  emit<K extends keyof Events & string>(name: K, ...args: PayloadArgs<Events[K]>): number {
    throw new Error("Not implemented");
  }

  listenerCount(name: keyof Events & string): number {
    throw new Error("Not implemented");
  }

  connect(handlers: Handlers<Events>): () => void {
    throw new Error("Not implemented");
  }

  next<K extends keyof Events & string>(name: K, options: NextOptions = {}): Promise<Events[K]> {
    throw new Error("Not implemented");
  }
}
```

**Test cases the backend runs**

**Test 1: Runs the start of opening night from the instructions** (visible)

```typescript
// The start of opening night from the instructions: listeners, emit, off and the counts.
import { CueBus } from "./solution.js";

type ShowEvents = {
  houseOpen: undefined;
  standby: { cue: number };
  cueGo: { cue: number; desk: "lights" | "sound" | "fly" };
  showStop: { reason: string };
};

const bus = new CueBus<ShowEvents>();
const log: unknown[] = [];
let houseOpened = 0;

bus.on("houseOpen", () => {
  houseOpened++;
});
const offLights = bus.on("cueGo", (payload) => log.push(["lights", payload]));
bus.on("cueGo", (payload) => log.push(["sound", payload]));

check.equal(bus.emit("houseOpen"), 1, "emit returns the number of listeners it called (houseOpen)");
check.equal(houseOpened, 1, "the houseOpen listener ran once");
check.equal(bus.emit("cueGo", { cue: 1, desk: "lights" }), 2, "emit returns the number of listeners it called (cueGo)");
check.equal(
  log,
  [
    ["lights", { cue: 1, desk: "lights" }],
    ["sound", { cue: 1, desk: "lights" }],
  ],
  "listeners run in the order they were added and receive the payload",
);
check.equal(bus.listenerCount("cueGo"), 2, "listenerCount counts the listeners of one event");

offLights();
check.equal(bus.listenerCount("cueGo"), 1, "the function returned by on removes that listener");
check.equal(bus.emit("standby", { cue: 2 }), 0, "emit returns 0 when nobody listens");
check.equal(bus.emit("cueGo", { cue: 2, desk: "sound" }), 1, "a removed listener is no longer called");
check.equal(log.length, 3, "only the remaining cueGo listener ran on the second cue");
```

**Test 2: Keeps registrations apart, applies changes from the next emit, and collects listener errors** (hidden)

```typescript
// Registrations, changes made during an emit, and listeners that throw.
import { CueBus } from "./solution.js";

type ShowEvents = {
  houseOpen: undefined;
  standby: { cue: number };
  cueGo: { cue: number; desk: "lights" | "sound" | "fly" };
  showStop: { reason: string };
};

const bus = new CueBus<ShowEvents>();

const reasons: string[] = [];
const note = (payload: { reason: string }): void => {
  reasons.push(payload.reason);
};
const offFirst = bus.on("showStop", note);
bus.on("showStop", note);
check.equal(bus.emit("showStop", { reason: "fire alarm" }), 2, "the same function added twice is two listeners");
check.equal(reasons, ["fire alarm", "fire alarm"], "each registration of the same function is called");
offFirst();
offFirst();
check.equal(bus.listenerCount("showStop"), 1, "off removes only its own registration, and a second call removes nothing");
check.equal(bus.listenerCount("houseOpen"), 0, "an event nobody listened to has no listeners");

const order: string[] = [];
let offSelf = (): void => {};
offSelf = bus.on("standby", (payload) => {
  order.push(`first ${payload.cue}`);
  offSelf();
  bus.on("standby", (later) => {
    order.push(`late ${later.cue}`);
  });
});
bus.on("standby", (payload) => {
  order.push(`second ${payload.cue}`);
});
check.equal(bus.emit("standby", { cue: 5 }), 2, "emit calls the listeners registered when it started");
check.equal(order, ["first 5", "second 5"], "a listener added during an emit is not called by that emit");
check.equal(bus.emit("standby", { cue: 6 }), 2, "the next emit sees listeners added and removed during the last one");
check.equal(order, ["first 5", "second 5", "second 6", "late 6"], "changes made during an emit apply from the next emit, in order");

const ran: string[] = [];
bus.on("cueGo", () => {
  ran.push("lights");
  throw new Error("lamp blown");
});
bus.on("cueGo", () => {
  ran.push("sound");
});
bus.on("cueGo", () => {
  ran.push("fly");
  throw new RangeError("fly bar stuck");
});
const failure = check.throws(
  () => bus.emit("cueGo", { cue: 7, desk: "fly" }),
  "emit throws an AggregateError when listeners throw",
  AggregateError,
);
check.equal(ran, ["lights", "sound", "fly"], "every listener runs even after an earlier one throws");
const errors = (failure as AggregateError).errors as Error[];
check.equal(errors.map((error) => error.message), ["lamp blown", "fly bar stuck"], "the AggregateError holds each thrown error, in order");
check.true(errors[1] instanceof RangeError, "the AggregateError keeps the original error objects");
```

**Test 3: Connects and disconnects a whole handler object** (hidden)

```typescript
// connect: one handler object for several events, and the function that disconnects it.
import { CueBus } from "./solution.js";

type ShowEvents = {
  houseOpen: undefined;
  standby: { cue: number };
  cueGo: { cue: number; desk: "lights" | "sound" | "fly" };
  showStop: { reason: string };
};

function counts(bus: CueBus<ShowEvents>): number[] {
  return [bus.listenerCount("houseOpen"), bus.listenerCount("standby"), bus.listenerCount("cueGo"), bus.listenerCount("showStop")];
}

const bus = new CueBus<ShowEvents>();
const seen: string[] = [];
const disconnect = bus.connect({
  onHouseOpen: () => {
    seen.push("house open");
  },
  onStandby: (payload) => {
    seen.push(`standby ${payload.cue}`);
  },
  onCueGo: (payload) => {
    seen.push(`go ${payload.cue} ${payload.desk}`);
  },
});
check.equal(counts(bus), [1, 1, 1, 0], "connect adds one listener for each handler it is given");

bus.emit("houseOpen");
bus.emit("standby", { cue: 12 });
bus.emit("cueGo", { cue: 12, desk: "lights" });
bus.emit("showStop", { reason: "interval" });
check.equal(seen, ["house open", "standby 12", "go 12 lights"], "each handler receives its own event and payload");

bus.on("cueGo", () => {
  seen.push("stage manager");
});
disconnect();
check.equal(counts(bus), [0, 0, 1, 0], "the returned function removes exactly the listeners connect added");
disconnect();
check.equal(counts(bus), [0, 0, 1, 0], "disconnecting twice removes nothing more");
bus.emit("cueGo", { cue: 13, desk: "fly" });
check.equal(seen.slice(3), ["stage manager"], "disconnected handlers are no longer called");

const second = bus.connect({ onShowStop: undefined, onStandby: (payload) => seen.push(`again ${payload.cue}`) });
check.equal(counts(bus), [0, 1, 1, 0], "connect skips handlers that are undefined");
bus.emit("standby", { cue: 14 });
check.equal(seen.at(-1), "again 14", "a handler connected later works like the first ones");
second();
check.equal(counts(bus), [0, 0, 1, 0], "the second connection disconnects on its own");
```

**Test 4: Waits for the next event and stops waiting when the signal is aborted** (hidden)

```typescript
// next: waiting for the next occurrence of an event, and cancelling the wait with an AbortSignal.
import { getEventListeners } from "node:events";
import { CueBus } from "./solution.js";

type ShowEvents = {
  houseOpen: undefined;
  standby: { cue: number };
  cueGo: { cue: number; desk: "lights" | "sound" | "fly" };
  showStop: { reason: string };
};

const bus = new CueBus<ShowEvents>();

const nextGo = bus.next("cueGo");
check.equal(bus.listenerCount("cueGo"), 1, "a waiting next counts as a listener");
check.equal(bus.emit("cueGo", { cue: 3, desk: "sound" }), 1, "emit counts a waiting next among the listeners it called");
check.equal(bus.listenerCount("cueGo"), 0, "next stops listening as soon as its event arrives");
bus.emit("cueGo", { cue: 4, desk: "sound" });
check.equal(await nextGo, { cue: 3, desk: "sound" }, "next resolves with the payload of the first emit after it was called");

const opened = bus.next("houseOpen");
const alsoOpened = bus.next("houseOpen");
check.equal(bus.emit("houseOpen"), 2, "two waiting calls to next are two listeners");
check.equal(await opened, undefined, "next resolves with undefined for an event without a payload");
check.equal(await alsoOpened, undefined, "one emit resolves every next that was waiting for it");

const controller = new AbortController();
const waiting = bus.next("standby", { signal: controller.signal });
const reason = new Error("show stopped");
controller.abort(reason);
check.equal(bus.listenerCount("standby"), 0, "aborting the signal stops next from listening at once");
const aborted = await check.rejects(() => waiting, "next rejects when its signal is aborted");
check.true(aborted === reason, "next rejects with the signal's reason");
check.equal(bus.emit("standby", { cue: 9 }), 0, "an aborted next is not called by later emits");

const finished = new AbortController();
finished.abort(new Error("too late"));
const late = bus.next("showStop", { signal: finished.signal });
check.equal(bus.listenerCount("showStop"), 0, "next with an already aborted signal never starts listening");
const lateError = await check.rejects(() => late, "next rejects at once when the signal is already aborted");
check.equal(lateError.message, "too late", "the rejection is the already aborted signal's reason");

const usher = new AbortController();
const seated = bus.next("standby", { signal: usher.signal });
check.equal(getEventListeners(usher.signal, "abort").length, 1, "next listens for abort on its signal while it waits");
bus.emit("standby", { cue: 10 });
check.equal(await seated, { cue: 10 }, "next with a signal resolves normally when the event comes first");
check.equal(getEventListeners(usher.signal, "abort").length, 0, "next removes its abort listener once it has resolved");
usher.abort(new Error("after the fact"));
check.equal(bus.listenerCount("standby"), 0, "aborting after next resolved changes nothing");
```

**Test 5: Derives exact types that reject misuse at compile time** (hidden)

```typescript
// Type-level tests: the types accept correct use and reject misuse. The misuse sits in
// functions that are never called, so it is only type-checked, never run.
import { CueBus, type Handlers, type PayloadArgs } from "./solution.js";

type Equal<A, B> = (<T>() => T extends A ? 1 : 2) extends <T>() => T extends B ? 1 : 2 ? true : false;
type Expect<T extends true> = T;

type ShowEvents = {
  houseOpen: undefined;
  standby: { cue: number };
  cueGo: { cue: number; desk: "lights" | "sound" | "fly" };
  showStop: { reason: string };
  note: string | undefined;
};

export type PayloadCases = [
  Expect<Equal<PayloadArgs<undefined>, []>>,
  Expect<Equal<PayloadArgs<{ cue: number }>, [payload: { cue: number }]>>,
  Expect<Equal<PayloadArgs<string | undefined>, [payload: string | undefined]>>,
];

export type HandlerCases = [
  Expect<Equal<keyof Handlers<ShowEvents>, "onHouseOpen" | "onStandby" | "onCueGo" | "onShowStop" | "onNote">>,
  Expect<Equal<Partial<Handlers<ShowEvents>>, Handlers<ShowEvents>>>,
];

export function correctUse(bus: CueBus<ShowEvents>): void {
  bus.emit("houseOpen");
  bus.emit("note", undefined);
  bus.emit("note", "house lights to half");
  bus.on("standby", (payload) => console.log(payload.cue + 1));
  bus.connect({ onCueGo: (payload) => console.log(payload.desk.toUpperCase()) });
  bus.connect({});
}

export function misuse(bus: CueBus<ShowEvents>): void {
  // @ts-expect-error cueGo needs its payload
  bus.emit("cueGo");
  // @ts-expect-error houseOpen carries no payload
  bus.emit("houseOpen", undefined);
  // @ts-expect-error the cue must be a number
  bus.emit("cueGo", { cue: "4", desk: "lights" });
  // @ts-expect-error there is no curtainUp event
  bus.emit("curtainUp");
  // @ts-expect-error the note event takes its argument even though it may be undefined
  bus.emit("note");
  // @ts-expect-error a standby payload has no desk
  bus.on("standby", (payload) => console.log(payload.desk));
  // @ts-expect-error there is no curtainUp event to handle
  bus.connect({ onCurtainUp: () => {} });
  // @ts-expect-error handler names are "on" plus the event name with a capital first letter
  bus.connect({ oncueGo: () => {} });
  // @ts-expect-error a houseOpen handler receives no payload
  bus.connect({ onHouseOpen: (payload: string) => console.log(payload) });
  // @ts-expect-error a cueGo handler receives a cueGo payload, not a standby one
  bus.connect({ onCueGo: (payload: { reason: string }) => console.log(payload.reason) });
}

export async function misuseNext(bus: CueBus<ShowEvents>): Promise<void> {
  const standby = await bus.next("standby");
  // @ts-expect-error a standby cue is a number
  const cue: string = standby.cue;
  console.log(cue);
}

check.true(typeof CueBus === "function", "the module exports the CueBus class");
```

The reference solution is [`content/tracks/typescript/advanced/lab/solution.ts`](../content/tracks/typescript/advanced/lab/solution.ts).

### Level IV · Professional: Production TypeScript

TypeScript that teams can build, ship and run. Configure tsconfig with the strictness that pays, structure monorepos with project references, build and bundle, publish packages with correct exports and declarations, lint with typed rules, write Node.js services, measure performance and memory, use streams and workers, keep code secure, and migrate JavaScript to TypeScript step by step.

**After this level you can**

- Configure tsconfig for TypeScript 7, including the strict flags and module settings that matter
- Structure, build and publish TypeScript projects and packages that work in ESM and CommonJS
- Lint with typed rules and test, and write Node.js services with validation and graceful shutdown
- Profile performance and memory, and use streams and worker threads
- Defend against the security mistakes types cannot catch, and migrate JavaScript incrementally

#### Lesson 1: tsconfig in Depth

*35 minutes.* Read and write a production tsconfig.json for TypeScript 7, know which defaults changed in TypeScript 6 and 7, add the checks beyond strict that pay for themselves, choose module settings, and recognize the options that are now errors.

**Objectives**

- Explain how tsc finds and reads tsconfig.json, and state the TypeScript 6 and 7 defaults
- Turn on noUncheckedIndexedAccess and exactOptionalPropertyTypes and fix the errors they report
- Use verbatimModuleSyntax and erasableSyntaxOnly to keep code safe for single-file tools and Node's type stripping
- Choose module settings for a Node.js app, a bundled app and a library, and replace removed options

**Outline**

1. What tsconfig.json controls
2. The defaults of TypeScript 6 and 7
3. The strict family and the checks beyond it
4. Flags for module syntax
5. Module and resolution choices
6. Options that are now errors
7. A production configuration

*35 minutes.* Separate type-checking from producing JavaScript, emit JavaScript, declarations and source maps with tsc, run TypeScript directly with Node's type stripping, and know what a bundler such as esbuild adds and leaves out.

#### Mock exam: Production TypeScript Mock Exam

*22 questions · 20 minutes · pass mark 70%.* Ten questions drawn from the level's bank, from tsconfig and builds to publishing, services, performance and security.

**Question 1** · One answer · `ts-professional-01`

A project has `@types/node` installed and this `tsconfig.json`:

```json
{ "compilerOptions": { "module": "nodenext" } }
```

`src/main.ts` contains `const port = process.env.PORT;`. What does TypeScript 7's `tsc` report?

- **✔ A. Error TS2591, cannot find name `process`: since TypeScript 6, `types` defaults to `[]`, so `@types/node` is not loaded until it is listed**
- B. Nothing: every installed `@types` package is loaded automatically
- C. An error because `strict` is off by default and `process.env` needs it
- D. An error because `module: nodenext` cannot be used without `moduleResolution: node`

> **Why:** TypeScript 6 changed the default of `types` to `[]`, and TypeScript 7 keeps it, so no
> `@types` package is included unless the config lists it. Add `"types": ["node"]`. The
> automatic loading in the second option was the old behavior. `strict` is now on by default,
> and `moduleResolution: node` (node10) has been removed; `nodenext` implies the matching
> resolution.

**Question 2** · One answer · `ts-professional-02`

With `"noUncheckedIndexedAccess": true`, which numbered line does the compiler reject?

```ts
const sizes = [10, 20, 30];
for (const size of sizes) console.log(size.toFixed(1)); // 2
const first = sizes[0];                                   // 3
console.log(first.toFixed(1));                            // 4
const counts: Record<string, number> = {};
counts["a"] = 1;                                          // 6
```

- **✔ A. Line 4 only: `first` is `number | undefined`, because an index may not exist**
- B. Lines 2 and 4: every element read from an array becomes possibly `undefined`
- C. Lines 4 and 6: writing to an index signature is also unchecked access
- D. None: the flag only affects objects with index signatures, not arrays

> **Why:** The flag adds `undefined` to values *read* by index, from arrays and from index signatures,
> so line 4 is `error TS18048: 'first' is possibly 'undefined'.` Iterating with `for...of`
> yields `number`, because iteration never visits a missing index. Writing `counts["a"] = 1`
> is allowed. The fix is a check or a default, such as `first?.toFixed(1) ?? "none"`.

**Question 3** · Select all that apply · `ts-professional-03`

Which of these `compilerOptions` entries make TypeScript 7 stop with an error saying the
option has been removed? Select all that apply.

- **✔ A. `"baseUrl": "./src"`**
- **✔ B. `"target": "es5"`**
- C. `"moduleResolution": "bundler"`
- D. `"verbatimModuleSyntax": true`

> **Why:** TypeScript 6 deprecated, and TypeScript 7 removed, `baseUrl` (error TS5102, "Option
> 'baseUrl' has been removed", with the hint to use `paths` relative to the config) and
> `target: es5` (error TS5108). Also removed: `moduleResolution` `node`/`node10` and
> `classic`, `outFile`, `downlevelIteration`, and the AMD, UMD and System module formats.
> `bundler` resolution and `verbatimModuleSyntax` are current, recommended settings.

**Question 4** · One answer · `ts-professional-04`

A monorepo's root `tsconfig.json` is:

```json
{
  "files": [],
  "references": [{ "path": "./packages/core" }, { "path": "./packages/cli" }]
}
```

Why is `"files": []` there?

- **✔ A. So the root compiles no files itself and only lists projects for `tsc -b`; without it the root would compile every file a second time**
- B. To mark the root as `composite`, which every referenced project requires
- C. To stop `tsc -b` from writing `.tsbuildinfo` files at the root
- D. Because an empty `files` array makes `tsc -b` build the references in parallel

> **Why:** This is a solution-style config. With no `files` or `include`, a config includes every
> `.ts` file under its folder, so the root would type-check and emit the packages' files
> again. `"files": []` (allowed when there are references) makes it an entry point only:
> `tsc -b` builds the referenced projects in dependency order. `composite` is set in the
> referenced projects themselves, and parallelism comes from TypeScript 7's `--builders`.

**Question 5** · One answer · `ts-professional-05`

`packages/cli` references `packages/core`. Everything is built. You edit a comment inside
the body of an exported function in the core and run `tsc -b --verbose`. What happens?

- **✔ A. The core is rebuilt; its `.d.ts` is unchanged, so the CLI is reported up to date with the declaration files of its dependencies and is not rechecked**
- B. Both projects are rebuilt, because the CLI depends on a project whose source changed
- C. Nothing is rebuilt, because comments never change the output
- D. Only the CLI is rebuilt, because it is the project that imports the changed function

> **Why:** Build mode compares each project's inputs with its `.tsbuildinfo`. The core's source changed,
> so the core is rebuilt. A dependent project reads its dependency through the emitted
> declaration files; since `index.d.ts` did not change, `tsc -b` prints that the CLI "is up to
> date with .d.ts files from its dependencies" and only updates its timestamps. A change to
> the core's public API would change the `.d.ts` and recheck the CLI.

**Question 6** · One answer · `ts-professional-06`

`src/oops.ts` contains:

```ts
const minutes: number = "ten";
console.log(minutes);
```

What does `node src/oops.ts` do on Node.js 26?

- **✔ A. It prints `ten`: Node strips the types and runs the rest without type-checking**
- B. It stops with error TS2322 before running anything
- C. It prints `NaN`, because the annotation converts the string to a number
- D. It refuses to run because `.ts` files need the `--experimental-transform-types` flag

> **Why:** Node's type stripping replaces annotations with spaces and executes the JavaScript that is
> left. It never checks types, so the wrong annotation is simply erased. Only `tsc` reports
> `error TS2322: Type 'string' is not assignable to type 'number'.`, which is why projects that
> run source directly still run `tsc --noEmit` in CI. Type stripping needs no flag, and
> `--experimental-transform-types` was removed in Node.js 26.

**Question 7** · Select all that apply · `ts-professional-07`

Which statements about bundling TypeScript with esbuild are true? Select all that apply.

- **✔ A. It does not type-check, so `tsc --noEmit` should run alongside it**
- **✔ B. It does not write `.d.ts` declaration files**
- **✔ C. It compiles each file on its own, so `isolatedModules` or `verbatimModuleSyntax` should be on**
- D. It calls TypeScript's programmatic API, so it must use TypeScript 6 until TypeScript 7.1

> **Why:** esbuild has its own TypeScript parser: it strips types without checking them and does not
> generate declarations, so a library still needs `tsc` (for example with
> `emitDeclarationOnly`). Because it sees one file at a time, it cannot tell whether an
> imported name is only a type; the two flags make `tsc` reject code it would mis-compile.
> Since it does not use TypeScript's API, TypeScript 7 lacking one does not affect it.

**Question 8** · One answer · `ts-professional-08`

Version 1.3.0 of a library exports `gradePercent(segment: Segment): number`. Which change
requires the next version to be 2.0.0?

- **✔ A. Changing the return type to `number | undefined` for zero-length segments**
- B. Adding a new exported function `climbEffort`
- C. Adding an optional second parameter `precision?: number`
- D. Fixing a rounding bug so that results match the documentation

> **Why:** Types are part of a TypeScript package's API. Widening a return type breaks every consumer
> that uses the result as a `number`: their code stops compiling, so it is a breaking change
> and a new MAJOR version. A new export and an optional parameter are compatible additions
> (MINOR); a bug fix that matches the documented behavior is a PATCH.

**Question 9** · One answer · `ts-professional-09`

`trail-grade` is an ESM-only package (`"type": "module"`, no top-level `await`). A
consumer's CommonJS file `report.cts` contains `import { gradePercent } from "trail-grade";`.
Which statement is correct?

- **✔ A. Under `module: nodenext` it compiles to a `require` call that works on Node.js 26; under `module: node16` it is error TS1479**
- B. It never works: CommonJS code can only load ESM packages with `await import()`
- C. It compiles under any `module` setting, but Node.js 26 throws `ERR_REQUIRE_ESM` at run time
- D. It works only if the package also publishes a CommonJS build under a `require` condition

> **Why:** Node.js can `require()` a synchronous ES module and returns its namespace object; the feature
> is no longer experimental. TypeScript models it under `nodenext` and `node20`. The older
> `node16` setting describes Node versions that could not, and reports error TS1479 ("the
> referenced file is an ECMAScript module and cannot be imported with 'require'"). This is why
> ESM-only packages can serve CommonJS consumers, as long as the package avoids top-level
> `await`, which would make `require()` fail with `ERR_REQUIRE_ASYNC_MODULE`.

**Question 10** · One answer · `ts-professional-10`

```ts
async function saveReading(celsius: number): Promise<void> {
  if (Number.isNaN(celsius)) throw new Error("reading is not a number");
  console.log(`saved ${celsius}`);
}

function onReading(raw: string): void {
  saveReading(Number(raw));
  console.log(`queued ${raw}`);
}

onReading("n/a");
```

`tsc` reports no errors. Which tool reports the bug before it runs?

- **✔ A. typescript-eslint's `no-floating-promises`, part of `recommendedTypeChecked`, which needs type information**
- B. typescript-eslint's `recommended` config, which needs only the syntax of the file
- C. `tsc` with `noUncheckedIndexedAccess` turned on
- D. Prettier with `--check`

> **Why:** The promise returned by `saveReading` is dropped, so its rejection is unhandled: the program
> prints `queued n/a` and then Node ends the process with the error. Knowing that the call
> returns a promise requires the type checker, so the rule is in the type-checked configs and
> needs `projectService: true`. Syntax-only rules cannot know it, no compiler flag forbids
> it, and Prettier only formats.

**Question 11** · One answer · `ts-professional-11`

A project builds with TypeScript 7 and wants typed linting with typescript-eslint. Why do
the TypeScript and Nx guides install `"typescript": "npm:@typescript/typescript6@^6.0.2"`
next to `"@typescript/native": "npm:typescript@^7.0.2"`?

- **✔ A. TypeScript 7.0 ships no programmatic API yet, so tools that import `typescript` get the 6.0 API under that name while `tsc` runs TypeScript 7**
- B. TypeScript 7 cannot read `tsconfig.json` files written for TypeScript 6
- C. ESLint only parses JavaScript, so TypeScript 6 converts the code to JavaScript first
- D. TypeScript 7 is slower at type-checking than TypeScript 6, so linting uses the faster version

> **Why:** TypeScript 7.0 does not ship an API (a new one is planned for 7.1), and typescript-eslint
> supports TypeScript below 6.1. The npm alias keeps the 6.0 API under the package name
> `typescript` that the plugins import, and the `@typescript/native` alias provides
> TypeScript 7's `tsc`. Both read the same `tsconfig.json`; TypeScript 7 is several times
> faster, not slower.

**Question 12** · One answer · `ts-professional-12`

A service calls `server.close()` on SIGTERM while one request is in flight. The request
finishes 100 ms later, yet the close callback runs only about three seconds after that.
The client is `fetch`. Why, and what is the fix?

- **✔ A. `fetch` keeps the connection alive after the response, and `close()` only closed the connections that were idle when it was called; send `connection: close` on responses written while shutting down**
- B. `close()` always waits for the server's `requestTimeout`; lower it to 100 ms
- C. The SIGTERM handler is missing `process.exit()`, which would close the connections
- D. The response was not flushed; call `response.flushHeaders()` before `end()`

> **Why:** Since Node.js 19, `server.close()` stops accepting connections and closes idle ones, but a
> keep-alive connection that becomes idle afterwards stays open until the client drops it.
> Sending `connection: close` while draining (or calling `closeIdleConnections()` after those
> responses) closes it at once. `process.exit()` would cut off in-flight requests instead of
> finishing them.

**Question 13** · One answer · `ts-professional-13`

```ts
const port = Number(process.env["PORT"] ?? 8080);
server.listen(port, "127.0.0.1");
```

The deployment sets `PORT=` (an empty value). What happens?

- **✔ A. `Number("")` is `0`, so the server listens on a random free port and nobody can reach it where expected**
- B. `??` treats the empty string as missing, so the server listens on 8080
- C. `Number("")` is `NaN`, so `listen` throws at startup
- D. TypeScript rejects the code because `process.env` values may be empty

> **Why:** `??` only replaces `null` and `undefined`, and an empty string is neither, so `Number("")`
> runs and returns `0`, which `listen` treats as "any free port". The program starts without
> complaint and silently listens on the wrong port. Parse configuration once at startup,
> reject empty and non-numeric values with a clear message, and refuse to start when anything
> is wrong.

**Question 14** · One answer · `ts-professional-14`

Both factories return objects that TypeScript types as `Order`. Which one gives V8 a
single hidden class for all orders, keeping property reads monomorphic?

```ts
function makeA(id: number, vip: boolean): Order {
  const order: Order = { id, total: 10 };
  if (vip) order.discount = 5;
  return order;
}

function makeB(id: number, vip: boolean): Order {
  return { id, total: 10, discount: vip ? 5 : undefined };
}
```

- **✔ A. `makeB`, because every object gets the same properties in the same order**
- B. `makeA`, because objects without a discount are smaller
- C. Both, because they return the same TypeScript type
- D. Neither, because object literals never share hidden classes

> **Why:** V8 gives objects that received the same properties in the same order one hidden class.
> `makeA` adds `discount` to some objects after creation, so orders come in two shapes, and
> code reading them becomes polymorphic. `makeB` always assigns all three properties.
> TypeScript's structural types say nothing about V8's shapes. (Checked with V8's
> `%HaveSameMap`: false for `makeA`'s two kinds of order, true for `makeB`'s.)

**Question 15** · One answer · `ts-professional-15`

A service runs under steady load. `process.memoryUsage().heapUsed`, read right after a
forced garbage collection at the end of each hour, is 31 MB, 58 MB, 91 MB, 120 MB. What is
the most likely explanation?

- **✔ A. A leak: something keeps references to objects it no longer needs, such as a cache with no limit**
- B. Normal behavior: the heap grows until the garbage collector runs
- C. The JIT compiler is optimizing more functions each hour
- D. The heap limit is too low and must be raised with `--max-old-space-size`

> **Why:** Memory that rises between collections and falls after them is normal. Here the readings are
> taken after a collection, so they show live objects, and the floor keeps rising: a leak.
> The usual cause in TypeScript services is an unintended reference: an unbounded cache, a
> listener never removed, a timer never cleared. Compare two heap snapshots to find it;
> raising the heap limit only delays the crash.

**Question 16** · One answer · `ts-professional-16`

```ts
const slowSink = new Writable({
  objectMode: true,
  highWaterMark: 2,
  write(reading: number, _encoding, done) {
    sleep(5).then(() => done(), done);
  },
});

let waits = 0;
for (let reading = 1; reading <= 6; reading++) {
  if (!slowSink.write(reading)) {
    waits += 1;
    await once(slowSink, "drain");
  }
}
console.log(waits);
```

What is printed?

- **✔ A. `3`**
- B. `0`
- C. `2`
- D. `6`

> **Why:** `write()` returns `false` when the buffered amount reaches the `highWaterMark`, here two
> objects. Readings 1 and 2 fill the buffer, so the second `write` returns `false` and the
> loop waits for `drain`, after which the buffer is empty again. The same happens at readings
> 4 and 6: three waits. Respecting `false` keeps memory bounded however many readings there
> are.

**Question 17** · One answer · `ts-professional-17`

A timer increments `ticks` every 10 ms. The program then counts primes below five million,
first by calling `countPrimes` directly, then by sending the work to a `Worker` and awaiting
its message. Each takes about 1.3 seconds. How many ticks happen during each?

- **✔ A. About 0 on the main thread and about 130 with the worker**
- B. About 130 in both cases, because timers have their own thread
- C. About 0 in both cases, because awaiting a worker also blocks the event loop
- D. About 130 on the main thread and 0 with the worker, because the worker takes the timer's thread

> **Why:** JavaScript runs on one thread around the event loop. A synchronous calculation occupies it,
> so no timer callback can run until it returns. A worker runs the calculation on another
> thread with its own event loop; the main thread only awaits a message, so its timers keep
> firing. In a real run: `main thread: 348513 primes, 0 ticks in 1309 ms` and
> `worker: 348513 primes, 140 ticks in 1423 ms`.

**Question 18** · One answer · `ts-professional-18`

```ts
interface Order {
  item: string;
  totalCents: number;
}

const order = JSON.parse('{ "item": "lamp", "totalCents": "4000" }') as Order;
const withShipping = order.totalCents + 500;
console.log(withShipping, typeof withShipping);
```

What does this print?

- **✔ A. `4000500 string`**
- B. `4500 number`
- C. Nothing: `tsc` rejects the assertion because `"4000"` is not a number
- D. Nothing: `as Order` throws a `TypeError` at run time

> **Why:** Types are erased, and `as` checks nothing at run time; the compiler simply believes it. At
> run time `totalCents` is the string `"4000"`, so `+` concatenates. Outside data must be
> treated as `unknown` and validated at the boundary before it gets a type.

**Question 19** · One answer · `ts-professional-19`

A settings endpoint deep-merges user JSON into defaults with a recursive `merge` that copies
every key from `Object.entries(source)`. An attacker sends:

```json
{ "theme": "dark", "__proto__": { "isAdmin": true } }
```

Afterwards, what does `({} as Record<string, unknown>)["isAdmin"]` evaluate to, in a
brand-new object anywhere in the process?

- **✔ A. `true`: `target["__proto__"]` is `Object.prototype`, so `isAdmin` was copied onto the prototype every object inherits from**
- B. `undefined`: `JSON.parse` drops keys named `__proto__`
- C. `undefined`: the polluted property exists only on the merged settings object
- D. It throws, because `Object.prototype` is frozen

> **Why:** `JSON.parse` creates an ordinary own key called `__proto__`, and `Object.entries` lists it.
> Reading `target["__proto__"]` returns `Object.prototype`, and the merge writes `isAdmin` into
> it, so every object now appears to have `isAdmin: true`. Defenses: validate with an allow
> list, keep user keys in a `Map` or `Object.create(null)` objects, skip `__proto__`,
> `constructor` and `prototype`, or run Node with `--disable-proto=delete`.

**Question 20** · One answer · `ts-professional-20`

```ts
function find(owner: string): unknown[] {
  return db.prepare(`SELECT code FROM parcels WHERE owner = '${owner}'`).all();
}
```

The table has three parcels, none owned by `nobody`. How many rows does
`find("nobody' OR '1'='1")` return, and what is the fix?

- **✔ A. 3 rows; use a placeholder, `prepare("SELECT code FROM parcels WHERE owner = ?").all(owner)`**
- B. 0 rows; the code is safe because `owner` is typed `string`
- C. 3 rows; escape single quotes with `owner.replaceAll("'", "")` and keep the template literal
- D. An error; SQLite refuses statements that contain `OR`

> **Why:** The template literal makes the input part of the SQL: `WHERE owner = 'nobody' OR '1'='1'`
> is true for every row. A `?` placeholder sends the value separately from the statement, so
> it is only ever data and matches nothing. The `string` type says nothing about the content.
> Hand-made escaping is easy to get wrong; placeholders are the fix every driver offers.

**Question 21** · One answer · `ts-professional-21`

A JavaScript file checked with `checkJs` contains:

```js
export const Band = { STANDARD: "standard", REDUCED: "reduced" };

/** @param {Band} band */
export function describe(band) {
  return String(band);
}
```

What does TypeScript 7 report?

- **✔ A. Error TS2749: 'Band' refers to a value, but is being used as a type here. Did you mean 'typeof Band'?**
- B. Nothing: in JSDoc, naming a value uses its type
- C. Error TS7006 only: parameters in JavaScript files always need explicit types
- D. Nothing: TypeScript 7 no longer checks JSDoc comments

> **Why:** TypeScript 7 analyzes JavaScript with the same rules as TypeScript, so a value cannot be
> used as a type in JSDoc any more; older versions quietly accepted it. Write
> `@param {typeof Band} band`, or define a `@typedef` such as
> `(typeof Band)[keyof typeof Band]`. JSDoc is still fully checked; `@enum`, `@class` on
> functions and Closure-style function types are among the other forms TypeScript 7 dropped.

**Question 22** · One answer · `ts-professional-22`

During a migration, a line carries `// @ts-expect-error legacy shape`. A later refactor fixes
the type error on that line but leaves the comment. What happens on the next `tsc` run?

- **✔ A. `tsc` reports error TS2578, an unused `@ts-expect-error` directive, so the stale suppression has to be removed**
- B. Nothing: the comment is ignored when there is no error to suppress
- C. `tsc` suppresses the next error that appears anywhere in the file
- D. The same as `// @ts-ignore`: both silently stay in the code

> **Why:** `@ts-expect-error` expects an error on the next line, and reports `error TS2578: Unused
> '@ts-expect-error' directive.` when there is none. That is why it is preferred over
> `@ts-ignore`, which stays silent forever. Combined with a counted budget in CI, it lets the
> number of suppressions only go down.

#### Lab: Kiln Booking Service

*TypeScript · about 60 minutes · 5 s per test.* Build a pottery studio's booking service in TypeScript, with typed configuration from the environment, field-by-field validation, structured errors, an HTTP server on 127.0.0.1 and a graceful shutdown, checked down to its types.

**Scenario**

Fireside Clay is a members' pottery studio with one electric kiln. Every Friday night the kiln is
loaded and fired, and members book shelf space in it during the week: how many pieces they bring,
how much they weigh, and the **cone**, the firing temperature their clay and glazes need (`06`
and `04` for low-fire earthenware, `6` for mid-fire stoneware, `10` for high-fire porcelain).
The kiln's shelves hold a fixed weight; once it is reached, the firing is full.

Bookings arrive from a small web form and a tablet by the kiln, both talking to a booking service
over HTTP. The current service was written in a weekend. It reads `process.env` in a dozen
places and starts happily with `KILN_PORT=eighty`, stores whatever JSON it is sent (one member's
"weight" was the string `"heavy"`), answers a typo in the body with a stack trace that once
showed the database password, and loses the booking being saved whenever the studio's host
restarts it to install updates.

You are writing its replacement in TypeScript: configuration parsed once and refused when wrong,
every booking validated field by field, one structured shape for every error, and a server that
finishes the requests it has started before it stops. The studio also wants the types to carry
the rules, so the web form's developers cannot send a cone that does not exist or read a booking
out of a failed validation.

**Instructions**

Write `solution.ts`. The starter declares every type, constant and function the tests import;
keep their names and signatures, and keep them exported. You may add functions, classes and
constants of your own. Do not start a server or read `process.env` at the top level: the tests
import your file and call what they need.

1. **Types.** Replace the three placeholders:
   - `Cone` is exactly one of the strings `"06"`, `"04"`, `"6"` and `"10"`.
   - `ErrorCode` is exactly one of `"invalid_body"`, `"invalid_json"`, `"payload_too_large"`,
     `"not_found"`, `"method_not_allowed"`, `"kiln_full"` and `"internal"`.
   - `ValidationResult` is a discriminated union: `{ readonly ok: true; readonly booking:
     BookingRequest }` or `{ readonly ok: false; readonly problems: readonly FieldProblem[] }`, so
     code can only read `booking` after checking `ok`.

   Tests check these types: a cone such as `"5"`, a code such as `"teapot"`, reading `booking`
   without checking `ok`, and assigning to a `Config` property must all be compile errors.
2. **`loadConfig(env)`** reads three variables from `env` (the tests pass plain objects; a real
   start would pass `process.env`). Spaces around a value are ignored.
   - `KILN_HOST`: default `"127.0.0.1"`; when set, it must not be empty.
   - `KILN_PORT`: default `8080`; when set, it must be written with digits only and be from `0`
     to `65535` (`0` means any free port). `"1e3"`, `"80.5"`, `"-1"` and `""` are problems.
   - `KILN_MAX_LOAD_KG`: default `60`; when set, digits with an optional decimal part such as
     `"72.5"`, above `0` and at most `500`.

   Check all three, then, if anything was wrong, throw **one** `ConfigError` whose `problems`
   lists one string per bad variable, in the order host, port, load. Each string starts with
   the variable's name and a space, for example `KILN_PORT must be a whole number from 0 to
   65535, got "eighty"`. Otherwise return the `Config`, frozen with `Object.freeze`.
3. **`validateBooking(body)`** checks a parsed JSON body of type `unknown`:
   - If `body` is not a plain object (it is `null`, an array, a string, a number or `undefined`),
     return `ok: false` with the single problem `{ field: "body", ... }`.
   - Otherwise check, in this order, and add one `{ field, problem }` per failing field:
     `member` (a string of 1 to 40 characters after trimming), `pieces` (a whole number from 1
     to 20), `weightKg` (a finite number above 0 and at most 25), `cone` (exactly one of the
     `Cone` strings). Then add a problem for every other key of the body, in the order the keys
     appear, with the key as `field`. The `problem` text is yours to word.
   - With no problems, return `ok: true` and a booking with the member's name trimmed.
4. **`errorResponse(status, code, message, details?)`** returns `{ status, body: { error: {
   code, message, details } } }`. Leave the `details` property out entirely when no details are
   given.
5. **`createHandler(config)`** returns a function that answers an `ApiRequest`. Each handler
   keeps its own list of bookings, starting empty. Paths match exactly, so `/firings/` is not
   `/firings`.

   | Request | Response |
   | --- | --- |
   | `GET /health` | `200`, `{ status: "ok" }` |
   | `GET /firings` | `200`, `{ bookings, loadKg, capacityKg }`: the accepted bookings in order, their total weight, and `config.maxLoadKg` |
   | `POST /firings`, body not valid | `400`, code `invalid_body`, the problems as `details` |
   | `POST /firings`, would make the load exceed `maxLoadKg` | `409`, code `kiln_full` (filling it exactly is allowed) |
   | `POST /firings`, otherwise | `201`, `{ booking }` with `id` `"B-1"`, `"B-2"`, ... counting accepted bookings only |
   | `/health` or `/firings` with another method | `405`, code `method_not_allowed` |
   | any other path | `404`, code `not_found` |

   Every error response is built with `errorResponse`; only `invalid_body` has `details`.
6. **`startServer(config, handler)`** serves `handler` (by default `createHandler(config)`) with
   `node:http` on `config.host` and `config.port`, and resolves once the server is listening,
   with a `RunningServer`:
   - `url` is `http://<host>:<port>` with the port the server really listens on, which matters
     when `config.port` is `0`.
   - For each request, call the handler with the method, the path from the URL without the query
     string, and the body: `undefined` when the body is empty, otherwise the parsed JSON.
   - A body larger than `MAX_BODY_BYTES` bytes is answered `413` with `payload_too_large`, and a
     body that is not valid JSON `400` with `invalid_json`; the handler is not called for either.
   - If the handler throws or its promise rejects, answer `500` with code `internal` and a
     generic message that does not contain the error's message (log it if you like), and keep
     serving.
   - Send every response body as JSON with the header `content-type: application/json;
     charset=utf-8`.
   - `close()` stops accepting connections at once, lets requests already in progress finish and
     receive their full responses, and resolves when the server has closed. It must resolve
     promptly after the last response even when the client keeps its connection alive, as
     `fetch` does. Lesson 6 shows the trap and its fix.

Example, a 30 kg kiln:

```ts
const handle = createHandler(loadConfig({ KILN_MAX_LOAD_KG: "30" }));
handle({ method: "GET", path: "/health", body: undefined });
// { status: 200, body: { status: "ok" } }
handle({ method: "POST", path: "/firings", body: { member: "  Ines Duarte ", pieces: 6, weightKg: 12.5, cone: "6" } });
// { status: 201, body: { booking: { id: "B-1", member: "Ines Duarte", pieces: 6, weightKg: 12.5, cone: "6" } } }
handle({ method: "POST", path: "/firings", body: { member: "Tomas", pieces: 4, weightKg: 15, cone: "06" } });
// 201, booking B-2; the load is now 27.5 kg
handle({ method: "POST", path: "/firings", body: { member: "Wen", pieces: 2, weightKg: 5, cone: "10" } });
// 409, { error: { code: "kiln_full", message: "..." } }
handle({ method: "POST", path: "/firings", body: { member: "Ade", pieces: 0, weightKg: 2, cone: "5" } });
// 400, { error: { code: "invalid_body", message: "...", details: [{ field: "pieces", ... }, { field: "cone", ... }] } }
handle({ method: "GET", path: "/firings", body: undefined });
// 200, { bookings: [B-1, B-2], loadKg: 27.5, capacityKg: 30 }

const server = await startServer(loadConfig({ KILN_PORT: "0" }));
const reply = await fetch(`${server.url}/health`);   // 200, {"status":"ok"}
await server.close();
```

**Tips.** Write the types first and let them guide the rest: once `ValidationResult` is a
discriminated union, the compiler tells you when you forget to check `ok`. Test `loadConfig`
with a value that `Number` accepts but the rules do not, such as `"1e3"`. For the server, start
from lesson 6: read the body with a limit, keep the handler's failures from reaching the client,
and remember that `server.listening` turns `false` as soon as `close()` is called.

**Boilerplate given to the learner** (`starter.ts`)

```typescript
import { createServer, type IncomingMessage } from "node:http";
import type { AddressInfo } from "node:net";

// ---------- Types ----------
// Step 1: make Cone, ErrorCode and ValidationResult as exact as the instructions describe.
// The placeholders below type-check, but they accept far too much.

export type Cone = string;

export type ErrorCode = string;

export type ValidationResult = {
  readonly ok: boolean;
  readonly booking?: BookingRequest;
  readonly problems?: readonly FieldProblem[];
};

// These types are complete.

export interface Config {
  readonly host: string;
  readonly port: number;
  readonly maxLoadKg: number;
}

export interface BookingRequest {
  readonly member: string;
  readonly pieces: number;
  readonly weightKg: number;
  readonly cone: Cone;
}

export interface Booking extends BookingRequest {
  readonly id: string;
}

export interface FieldProblem {
  readonly field: string;
  readonly problem: string;
}

export interface ApiRequest {
  readonly method: string;
  readonly path: string;
  readonly body: unknown;
}

export interface ApiResponse {
  readonly status: number;
  readonly body: unknown;
}

export type Handler = (request: ApiRequest) => ApiResponse | Promise<ApiResponse>;

export interface RunningServer {
  readonly url: string;
  close(): Promise<void>;
}

export const MAX_BODY_BYTES = 16_384;

export class ConfigError extends Error {
  readonly problems: readonly string[];
  constructor(problems: readonly string[]) {
    super(`invalid configuration: ${problems.join("; ")}`);
    this.name = "ConfigError";
    this.problems = problems;
  }
}

// ---------- Configuration ----------

// Step 2: read KILN_HOST, KILN_PORT and KILN_MAX_LOAD_KG; throw one ConfigError listing every problem.
export function loadConfig(env: Readonly<Record<string, string | undefined>>): Config {
  throw new Error("Not implemented");
}

// ---------- Validation ----------

// Step 3: check an unknown request body field by field.
export function validateBooking(body: unknown): ValidationResult {
  throw new Error("Not implemented");
}

// ---------- Handler ----------

// Step 4: the one shape every error response has.
export function errorResponse(
  status: number,
  code: ErrorCode,
  message: string,
  details?: readonly FieldProblem[],
): ApiResponse {
  throw new Error("Not implemented");
}

// Step 5: GET /health, GET /firings and POST /firings, with this handler's own bookings.

  throw new Error("Not implemented");
}

// ---------- Server ----------

// Step 6: serve a handler over HTTP; read bodies with a limit; close gracefully.
// createServer, IncomingMessage and AddressInfo are imported above for you.
```
